checks.claim: Only Wokwi runs the compiled ESP32-S3 Arduino firmware with LEDC, GPIO input, esp_timer, TWDT, host serial link and automation together
checks.source: (comparative claim; nothing in the Wokwi sources can confirm or refute it)
checks.correction: This needs the QEMU/Renode/esp-emu findings. Note that Espressif's new pytest-embedded-espemu (2.9.0, 2026-08-25) supports only RISC-V targets, not S3 (https://github.com/espressif/pytest-embedded/tree/main/pytest-embedded-espemu).

missed_facts.candidate: Wokwi Python Client / pytest-embedded-wokwi / Wokwi CI Server
missed_facts.fact: wokwi-client (every version up to 0.4.0) ignores WOKWI_CLI_SERVER in WokwiClient/WokwiClientSync: 'Transport(token, server or DEFAULT_WS_URL)'. pytest-embedded-wokwi 2.8.1 and 2.9.3 call WokwiClientSync(token) with no server. Any Python or pytest use of a self-hosted wokwi-ci-server therefore needs an explicit server= argument or a patch; otherwise it silently uses the cloud and its quota.

LEDC has no public automated regression test on Wokwi. esp32-test-binaries builds ESP-IDF's ledc test app for all chips, but there is no test_ledc.py and no 'ledc' entry in the nightly matrix. arduino-esp32 also skips its adc_pwm suite, including the LEDC cases, on Wokwi. The LEDC 'yes' rests on the docs tick and closed user bug reports, so the first experiment must measure the 1000-2000 us / 50 Hz pulses from a VCD.

The ESP-IDF esp_timer test app runs on Wokwi only for esp32c3 (test_timer.py). On S3, esp_timer is covered only by arduino-esp32's Ticker test, which runs in the cloud. The S3 nightlies do include gptimer (cpuFrequency 16) and task_wdt.

PCNT on esp32s3 is exercised by Wokwi's nightly ESP-IDF pulse_cnt tests (all Unity cases), which helps the future encoder driver. Wokwi also has a built-in KY-040 rotary encoder part (CLK/DT quadrature, 20 steps/rev, click or keyboard only, no automation controls) and a clock-generator part. Both can feed PCNT before a custom MT6701/encoder chip exists.

Espressif's own script comment in PR #12875 says 'Local and Wokwi use USB Serial/JTAG, so Enabled (CDCOnBoot=cdc)'; UART0 in CI is only for the hardware runners. This is the best available public hint that Arduino HWCDC (3.3.x, P4) works on Wokwi's USB-Serial-JTAG model. In contrast, the ESP-IDF usb_serial_jtag test app that passes on S3 never exercises the SOF-based connection check that 2.0.17's HWCDC depends on.

The JS client supports server-side pause points of type 'serial-bytes' (pause the simulation exactly when a byte sequence is emitted), besides time-relative and time-absolute ones. wokwi-client (Python) exposes only time-based pausing (resume pause_after, wait_until_simulation_time). For lock-stepping the COBS protocol to simulated time, the JS client is currently more capable.

Empirical check on this machine: the real @wokwi/rfc2217 server code from wokwi-cli v0.27.1 was compiled with tsc and paired with a local echo in place of the simulator. pyserial 3.5 from D:/xetulai/autopark/autopark/.venv connected via serial_for_url('rfc2217://localhost:47001') in 0.37 s, and a 1032-byte payload with all 256 byte values came back byte-identical. The server listens on all interfaces, since listen(port) is called with no host.
missed_facts.source: https://github.com/wokwi/wokwi-cli/blob/v0.27.1/packages/rfc2217/src/RFC2217Server.ts ; local test script in the scratchpad (rfc_test/client_test.py)

missed_facts.fact: arduino-esp32 pins wokwi/wokwi-ci-server-action to its initial 2024-06-04 commit a6fabb5, which runs the container without -e GITHUB_ACTIONS=1. That variable was only added to v1 on 2026-02-05. There is no public evidence that set-control, pin reads, VCD export or GDB work on the self-hosted image; the CLI-based nightlies that use it only wait for and write serial text.

The pricing page (Community €0 'For open source projects', Hobby €5.6, Hobby+ €8.1, Pro €20/seat, annual billing) lists CI minutes only for Pro (2000/month). The Free 50 and Hobby/Hobby+ 200 minute quotas appear only in the docs. The ToS (last updated 2026-04-14) also forbid 'Using the Service at no cost for commercial purposes' without Wokwi's consent.

missed_facts.candidate: Wokwi for VS Code / Wokwi CLI
missed_facts.fact: The S3 GDB for Wokwi debugging already exists locally at D:/xetulai/_platformio/core/packages/toolchain-xtensa-esp32s3/bin/xtensa-esp32s3-elf-gdb.exe. The Wokwi docs' PlatformIO example path points at the classic-ESP32 toolchain under ~/.platformio and would not work here.
missed_facts.source: https://docs.wokwi.com/vscode/debugging ; local directory listing of D:/xetulai/_platformio/core/packages

missed_facts.fact: --quiet does not suppress simulated serial output. Serial bytes are always written to stdout, while --serial-log-file only adds a copy, so a binary COBS session will print raw bytes to the console unless stdout is redirected.
Version 0.11.0 raised the minimum supported IntelliJ Platform to 2026.2, so older CLion/RustRover installs cannot use it.

Wokwi's own nightly workflow ('Test in Wokwi', daily cron 05:42 UTC) is currently green, runs #1061-#1065, including the S3 task_wdt, usb_serial_jtag, pcnt, gptimer, uart and gpio jobs. The arduino-esp32 runtime report header meanwhile reads 'The test workflows are failing', because its hardware columns are cached last-success results.

verification.overall:
Most of the report holds up against primary sources. The engine capability table, cpuFrequency cap, USB_SERIAL_JTAG attribute, logic analyzer and pushbutton behaviour all check out. So do nearly all version and date numbers: VS Code 3.7.0 (2026-08-28), CLI v0.27.1 (2026-09-16) with v0.20/0.21/0.23 feature dates, wokwi-client 0.4.0 (2026-02-19), pytest-embedded-wokwi 2.9.3 (2026-08-31), IntelliJ 0.11.0 (2026-09-04), the Docker tag 20260927, the arduino-esp32 report of 2026-09-29, PR #12875 merged 2026-09-15, and the prices, quotas, licenses and ToS terms.

Errors that matter for feasibility:
(1) wokwi-client ignores WOKWI_CLI_SERVER unless server= is passed. pytest-embedded-wokwi never passes it, so arduino-esp32's Wokwi pytest jobs (Arduino S3 results, the gpio button test, the i2c test) almost certainly ran on the Wokwi cloud, not the self-hosted wokwi-ci-server. The report's evidence that the self-hosted server supports control:set, I2C and Arduino tests is therefore invalid. The report's line that the Python serial API works with any WOKWI_CLI_SERVER is wrong, and so is the Python summary's claim that WOKWI_CLI_SERVER changes the server.
(2) wokwi/flasher-esp32 and MabezDev/wokwi-server are not archived.
(3) CLI -q does not silence binary serial echo on stdout.
(4) The -g flag arrived in v0.27.1, not v0.27.0.
(5) The Python client does use TCP: a WebSocket to wss://wokwi.com by default.

Nuances:
- PR #12875 forces UART0 in CI because of the hardware runners, and Espressif explicitly runs HWCDC on Wokwi locally (P4). That is weak positive evidence for HWCDC. The IDF USJ test that passes on S3 does not exercise the SOF check, so 2.0.17 HWCDC on S3 remains untested and still needs a smoke test.
- LEDC has no public automated Wokwi regression test on any chip, so pulse widths must be verified from a VCD in the first experiment.

Positive, independently verified:
- The CLI's RFC2217 bridge code is byte-transparent with pyserial 3.5 (local test: all 256 byte values round-trip; connects in 0.37 s).
- SerialVehicleIO only needs write/in_waiting/read/close.

Could not verify:
- Cloud latency and whether cloud runs are real-time throttled.
- Whether billing counts simulated or wall-clock minutes.
- Self-hosted server terms.
- The comparative 'only Wokwi' claim.

report.topic: Espressif QEMU and QEMU-based front-ends for running the autopark ESP32-S3 Arduino firmware without hardware (checked 2026-09-29)

candidates.name: Espressif QEMU fork (qemu-system-xtensa -machine esp32s3), including the ESP-IDF 'idf.py qemu' front-end
candidates.license: GPL-2.0 (QEMU as a whole). Espressif mask-ROM images (pc-bios/esp32s3_rev0_rom.bin etc.) ship as binary blobs. The idf.py qemu front-end is part of ESP-IDF (Apache-2.0).
candidates.latest_version: esp-develop-9.2.2-20260417 (QEMU 9.2.2). GitHub release published 2026-04-19, tagged 2026-04-17; the latest Espressif release as of 2026-09-29. The esp-develop head (2026-04-29) has no USB-JTAG, LEDC, I2C or WDT changes. ESP-IDF master tools.json recommends esp_develop_9.2.2_20260417 for esp32/esp32s3.
candidates.summary: Espressif's QEMU fork emulates ESP32, ESP32-C3 and, since esp-develop-9.0.0-20240606, ESP32-S3. The S3 model includes dual-core LX7, the ROM, SPI flash (2/4/8/16 MB), PSRAM (-m), UART0/1, the interrupt matrix, SysTimer, timer groups, eFuse, RNG, crypto, GDMA and TWAI. It also has SD/MMC on S3 (since 20260417), an OpenCores Ethernet MAC and a virtual RGB framebuffer. It boots a merged flash image with -drive file=...,if=mtd,format=raw, can expose a UART over TCP, and has a GDB stub and QMP/HMP control. Hands-on on this machine (29/09/2026): the project firmware (Arduino-ESP32 2.0.17, Serial moved to UART0) passed the protocol, state-machine, timeout, reconnect, reset-reason and panic-hook checks through SerialVehicleIO over socket://.

capabilities.detail: The whole emulator is GPL-2.0 on GitHub, with device models in hw/xtensa/esp32s3.c, hw/timer/esp_timg.c and related files. Only the bundled Espressif ROM images are binary blobs. Espressif states that it 'does not provide support for QEMU', so issues are handled best-effort.

Machine 'esp32s3' ('Espressif ESP32S3 machine', 2 CPUs by default). History: initial S3 support in esp-develop-9.0.0-20240606; quad/octal PSRAM, virtual RGB LCD and SHA-384/512 in 9.2.2-20250228; S3 SD/MMC and TIE-instruction fixes in 9.2.2-20260417. Hands-on 29/09/2026: the repo firmware boots and runs on it.

Hands-on: the Arduino-ESP32 2.0.17 app (PlatformIO espressif32 7.1.3) runs unchanged, except that Serial must be on UART0 (-DARDUINO_USB_CDC_ON_BOOT=0). A QIO build written as an 8 MB image boot-loops, because the gd25q64 flash model QEMU picks for 8 MB lacks the quad-enable bit; it boots from a 16 MB image (is25lp128 model) or as a DIO build. Arduino-ESP32 3.x on S3 has not been run here (CHƯA THỬ). arduino-esp32's own docs say 'QEMU is only supported for ESP32 and ESP32-C3 targets'.

Neither platformio/platform-espressif32 7.1.3 nor pioarduino 55.03.312 mentions QEMU (repos checked 2026-09). It still works from .pio/build outputs. Merge the binaries with esptool: merge_bin --fill-flash-size on v4, or merge-bin --pad-to-size on v5. Layout: bootloader.bin@0x0, partitions.bin@0x8000, boot_app0.bin@0xe000, firmware.bin@0x10000. Pass the result with -drive if=mtd (hands-on). PlatformIO's generic test_testing_command, documented with qemu-riscv/HiFive1, could run 'pio test' inside QEMU (CHƯA THỬ).

UART0 and UART1 are wired to QEMU chardevs (serial_hd(0) and serial_hd(1)); UART2 is not. The option -serial tcp::5555,server,nowait works with pyserial serial_for_url('socket://127.0.0.1:5555') (documented; hands-on: 20 Hz telemetry, 0 frame errors). QEMU docs also offer the Windows-only -serial COMn (host COM port, e.g. a com0com pair); CHƯA THỬ. Caveat: pyserial's socket:// in_waiting only returns 0 or 1 because it is select-based, so a non-blocking poll loop needs a draining adapter (hands-on).

There is only a register stub, 'misc.esp32c3.usb_serial_jtag', at 0x60038000. Reads return 0, writes are dropped, and it has no chardev; the esp-develop head of 2026-04-29 is the same. The docs table marks USB ❌ on all targets. As a result the HWCDC Serial of the unmodified firmware cannot be reached (hands-on: a HELLO sent on UART0 got 0 bytes back).

The docs mark LEDC ❌ for ESP32-S3. Its registers fall inside the generic 'esp32s3.iomem' region, where reads return 0 and writes are ignored silently. Only the classic ESP32 machine has an LEDC model, and it only passes an integer duty % to QEMU LED devices, with no period or pulse timing. ESC and servo pulse widths cannot be observed.

The GPIO model implements only GPIO_STRAP; every other register reads 0 and writes are ignored. The docs mark the GPIO matrix/IOMUX ❌. There is no host API to drive a pin. The E-stop input (INPUT_PULLUP, open circuit = pressed) therefore always reads LOW, i.e. 'not pressed', so the E-stop path is bypassed without any warning.

The docs mark I2C, GP-SPI, I2S and RMT ❌; ADC, PCNT and MCPWM are not in the supported list. The esp32s3 machine creates no I2C or SPI2 controller. The classic ESP32 machine does have an undocumented I2C controller with a TMP105 hard-wired at 0x48. Sensors such as AS5600, BNO085, VL53L1X and MT6701 would each need a new C device model.

Works (hands-on): SysTimer (esp_timer), timer groups, RNG, panic → backtrace → reboot, esp_restart, and reset reasons POWER_ON, PANIC and SOFTWARE; __wrap_esp_panic_handler is called. The timer-group watchdogs never fire on esp32s3. The cause: esp_timg.c latches the stage config only when CONF_UPDATE_EN (bit 22) is set, but S3 silicon has no such bit (WDTCONFIG0 bits 21-22 are reserved), and IDF's S3 HAL never sets it (v4.4, v5.5 and master); the C3 HAL does. The RTC WDT is not emulated. The model keeps peripheral state across a CPU-only reset, but LEDC is absent, so 'PWM keeps running after a CPU reset' cannot be checked, and the panic hook's GPIO writes are invisible. Time is QEMU_CLOCK_VIRTUAL tied to the host clock (no -icount by default): about 0.1-0.17 % slow, with rare host stalls over 100 ms (hands-on). -icount gives deterministic but not cycle-accurate time; CHƯA THỬ on S3.

Headless (-nographic) with a TCP serial port, a GDB stub (-s -S) and QMP/HMP (system_reset, register reads). pytest-embedded-qemu can drive it. The ESP-IDF Docker image installs qemu* through idf_tools; ESP-IDF's pytest.ini defines a 'qemu' marker; arduino-esp32 has a GitHub Actions QEMU job on ubuntu-latest, currently disabled. No account, token or paid plan. esptool cannot reset over TCP because RTS is not transmitted, so use system_reset or QMP. QEMU writes flash changes back into the image file, so use a fresh copy per run.

Every release ships an official x86_64-w64-mingw32 tarball, and ESP-IDF tools.json has a win64 entry. The 20260417 release removed the runtime dependency on libiconv-2.dll. Hands-on 29/09/2026 on Windows 11: the static binary runs with no install or admin rights, about 174 MB unpacked; it used about 108 % of one core and 55 MB RAM.

QEMU itself only emulates, but the same host-side tests can target both. The project's SerialVehicleIO accepts socket:// (QEMU) or a COM port (board), and pytest-embedded can switch between its 'qemu' service and the 'esp'/serial services. esptool and espefuse also work against QEMU over socket:// when it boots in UART download strap mode.

candidates.fit: This is the best open-source, free, native-Windows option in this area, and it is already proven on this project: protocol, timeouts, reconnect, reset reasons and the panic hook all worked with a UART0 build variant. It fits well as a CI 'firmware-in-the-loop' stage for the main.cpp glue and the protocol, next to the 703 host checks. On ESP32-S3 it cannot validate the USB-CDC transport, LEDC PWM, the E-stop GPIO, I2C/SPI sensors, ADC/PCNT or watchdog timeouts. Those still need host-side fakes and the real board.
caveats: A QEMU-only PlatformIO env is required (-DARDUINO_USB_CDC_ON_BOOT=0); the production USB-CDC build cannot be reached from the host.
A QIO build on an 8 MB image boot-loops. Use a 16 MB image or a DIO build. Only 2, 4, 8 and 16 MB images are accepted.

The S3 timer-group WDT never fires because of the CONF_UPDATE_EN latch, which does not match S3 silicon. This looks like an upstream bug worth reporting. The docs still name 'timer.esp32c3.timg', while the release uses 'timer.esp32s3.timg'. idf.py qemu passes timer.<target>.timg wdt_disable=true by default.
The E-stop always reads 'not pressed' and LEDC writes are discarded, so QEMU runs must not be counted as E-stop or PWM coverage.
Time follows the host clock: host stalls can latch LOOP_OVERRUN, and millis() is not reset by emulated resets.
The flash image is modified in place (a panic writes a core dump), so copy the image for each run.
The docs (esp-toolchain-docs, last changed 2025-09-11 and 2025-08-29) are older than the binary; the S3 SD/MMC row is out of date.

idf.py qemu (in code since ESP-IDF v5.3, S3 documented since v5.4, stable docs v6.1) needs an ESP-IDF project build directory, so it is not directly usable for this PlatformIO/Arduino project; call qemu-system-xtensa directly.
candidates.cost_notes: Free (GPL-2.0) with no account. About 174 MB of disk for the Windows build. Best-effort community support only.

candidates.name: pytest-embedded (Espressif) with the pytest-embedded-qemu, -serial-esp and -arduino services
candidates.license: MIT
candidates.latest_version: 2.9.3 (2026-08-31, PyPI/GitHub). Requires Python ≥3.10. pytest-embedded-qemu depends on qemu.qmp==0.0.3.
candidates.summary: Espressif's pytest plugin family. The 'qemu' service starts QEMU with a merged image (options --qemu-image-path, --qemu-prog-path, --qemu-cli-args, --qemu-extra-args, --qemu-efuse-path), reads the console from QEMU stdio and resets through QMP. The 'esp'/serial services run the same test functions on a real board. Both ESP-IDF (pytest 'qemu' marker) and arduino-esp32's runtime tests use it.

capabilities.detail: MIT-licensed, per the package LICENSE and PyPI classifier.
QEMU_TARGETS includes esp32s3 (strap 0x07 and a default eFuse image); the default CLI format is '-nographic -machine {target}'.
A pytest-embedded-arduino service exists. arduino-esp32's tests run with '--embedded-services esp,arduino,wokwi,qemu' and pin version 2.8.1.

There is no PlatformIO service. The qemu service accepts any merged image through --qemu-image-path. For a real board you would flash with pio and then use the serial service without auto-flash (CHƯA THỬ).

The QEMU DUT reads QEMU stdout and writes to its stdin (DuplicateStdoutPopen), and uses QMP for control. Its matching is text/regex-based (pexpect), so binary COBS frames would need custom handling. Alternatively, --qemu-extra-args can add '-serial tcp::…' so the project's SerialVehicleIO talks to the device directly.
Inherits the QEMU limitation: USB-Serial-JTAG is only a stub.
No pin or PWM API; LEDC is not modelled on S3 in QEMU.
No API to drive GPIO; the QEMU GPIO model is strap-only.
No device models of its own, and QEMU has no I2C on S3.
hard_reset() sends QMP system_reset, and panic text can be matched with expect(). Watchdog and timing limits come from QEMU.
pytest CLI with JUnit XML; used in ESP-IDF and arduino-esp32 CI. No account needed.

The PyPI classifier says 'OS Independent', but the qemu service depends on QEMU console stdio, and its eFuse helper uses pexpect.spawn, which pexpect documents as unavailable on Windows. No Windows CI evidence was found (CHƯA THỬ).
The same test module can run against a real board with the serial/esp services; arduino-esp32 runs identical tests on hardware, Wokwi and QEMU.

candidates.fit: A good fit for the 'one test suite for simulation and board' requirement. The pattern (merged image → QEMU → pytest, then the same tests → COM port) is exactly what Espressif and arduino-esp32 use. For this project's binary protocol, keep SerialVehicleIO as the protocol client and use pytest(-embedded) only for lifecycle work: starting QEMU, QMP reset and log capture. Its QEMU service on Windows is unverified.
caveats: It adds no peripheral coverage; it inherits every QEMU limitation.
Its DUT abstraction is text/expect-oriented, not framed-binary.
arduino-esp32 pins 2.8.1, while the latest is 2.9.3 (2026-08-31).

candidates.name: arduino-esp32 runtime-test pipeline (tests_run.sh -Q + tests_qemu.yml), a reference harness
candidates.license: LGPL-2.1 (arduino-esp32 repository)
candidates.latest_version: master @6cddb194 (2026-09-29). Latest core 3.3.12 (2026-09-18) on ESP-IDF v5.5.5; 4.0.0-RC1 (2026-09-23) on ESP-IDF v6.1. Pins pytest-embedded(-qemu) 2.8.1 and esptool 5.3.1.
candidates.summary: Espressif's own example of testing Arduino sketches in QEMU. It builds <sketch>.ino.merged.bin and downloads the latest espressif/qemu Linux release. It then runs pytest-embedded with '--embedded-services qemu', '--qemu-image-path …merged.bin' and '--qemu-cli-args "-machine $target -m 4M -nographic"'; RISC-V targets add '-icount 3'. As of 2026-09-29 the QEMU stage is disabled ('redundant with most of the Wokwi tests') and covers only esp32 and esp32c3.

capabilities.detail: The CI scripts and workflows live in the LGPL-2.1 arduino-esp32 repository.
QEMU_TEST_TARGETS contains only 'esp32' and 'esp32c3', and the docs say 'QEMU is only supported for ESP32 and ESP32-C3 targets'.
It tests the Arduino core itself (3.x master) using the sketches' merged binaries.
It builds with the Arduino toolchain (arduino-cli/sketch_utils); PlatformIO is not used.
The console is read through pytest-embedded from QEMU stdio; there is no TCP serial port in this harness.
Not supported; QEMU has only a stub.
The adc_pwm test and other peripheral tests set 'qemu: false' in their ci.yml.
tests/validation/gpio/ci.yml sets 'qemu: false'.
tests/validation/i2c_master/ci.yml sets 'qemu: false'.
Only the timer, ticker, hash, fs, unity, multitasking and hello_world tests are eligible for QEMU (they have no 'qemu: false'), and only on esp32/esp32c3.

A full GitHub Actions flow exists: it caches the latest QEMU release, downloads binaries from the build job and uploads JUnit results. It is currently switched off (qemu_enabled=false) because Wokwi 'can cover most of what QEMU does'.
As shipped it uses bash scripts, an ubuntu-latest runner and the x86_64-linux-gnu QEMU tarball.
The same pytest files run on physical boards (GitLab lab), on Wokwi and on QEMU; each test's ci.yml enables or disables platforms.

candidates.fit: Useful only as a template: merged image + pytest-embedded + per-test ci.yml flags such as 'qemu: false', plus a runner switch between hardware, Wokwi and QEMU. It does not cover ESP32-S3 in QEMU and is currently turned off in favour of Wokwi and hardware.
caveats: Disabled by default as of 2026-09-29.
ESP32 and ESP32-C3 only.

candidates.name: PICSimLab (with lcgamboa's qemu-esp32 'picsimlab-esp32' backend)
candidates.license: GPL-2.0 (PICSimLab COPYING); the QEMU backend fork is GPL-2.0.
candidates.latest_version: 0.9.3 (released 2026-09-20). Backend: lcgamboa/qemu branch picsimlab-esp32, last commit 2026-09-19 ('Updated to use qemu-esp32 0.9.2'). Python client PICSimLab-rcontrol 0.9.2 (2026-06-20).
candidates.summary: A real-time board simulator GUI with spare parts (sensors, displays, oscilloscope, VCD dump). Its ESP32 boards run on lcgamboa's QEMU fork, whose esp32-picsimlab machine has callbacks for GPIO, I2C, SPI, UART, RMT, LEDC and ADC. Supported ESP32 boards are ESP32_DevKitC and ESP32_C3_DevKitC_02 only; there is no ESP32-S3.

capabilities.detail: PICSimLab and its QEMU fork are both GPL-2.0 on GitHub.
The 0.9.3 board list contains only ESP32_C3_DevKitC_02 and ESP32_DevKitC. The fork's hw/xtensa has esp32_picsimlab.c but no S3 picsimlab machine; its esp32s3.c is Espressif's stock machine.

Arduino IDE and VSCode+PlatformIO project-wizard templates exist for ESP32/ESP32-C3 (0.9.3), but only for those chips. Only DIO/DOUT flash modes are supported ('Qemu ESP32 don't support the QIO and QOUT flash modes').

picsimlab_tool loads .bin/.hex into a running simulator and is described as usable 'integrated in development tools (like platformio)'. Project-wizard templates exist for Vscode+PlatformIO, but only for classic ESP32/C3.

The simulated UART connects to a host COM port through a null-modem emulator (com0com on Windows, tty0tty on Linux), 8N1. The other end can be opened by pyserial or esptool, which can flash 'as a real ESP32 board'.
No S3 support; USB-Serial-JTAG is not documented for its boards.
ESP32/C3 only: LEDC PWM output with settable frequency, an oscilloscope with measurements (rcontrol 'oscmeasures') and VCD Dump parts. Not available for S3.
ESP32/C3 only: parts such as buttons and switches can be set through rcontrol 'set obj value'; 'pins'/'pinsl' show pin states.

ESP32/C3 only. I2C/SPI parts include MPU6050 (raw values only), ADXL345, BMP180/280, SHT3X, DS1621, 24CXXX, MCP23017, PCF8574 and SSD1306, plus HC-SR04 and rotary-encoder parts. There is no AS5600, BNO085 or VL53L1X.
ESP32/C3 only, on the Espressif-derived QEMU. Options include enabling/disabling the watchdog (ESP32-C3), icount=auto, and sim stop/start. Not applicable to S3.

The rcontrol text protocol runs over TCP (default port 5000, up to 4 connections) with commands such as set/get, pins, reset, loadhex, sync and oscmeasures. A Python wrapper is on PyPI (PICSimLab-rcontrol). 0.9.3 publishes a Linux 'PICSimLab_NOGUI' AppImage, which is not documented. It is mainly a GUI app.
The 0.9.3 release includes win64 setup.exe and zip builds.
Simulator only; the rcontrol tests do not apply to a real board.

candidates.fit: Not usable for this firmware: there is no ESP32-S3 board, and the firmware targets S3 with USB-CDC. Its strengths (driveable GPIO, LEDC oscilloscope, I2C parts, TCP remote control) apply only to classic ESP32 and ESP32-C3. At most it could inspire a way of driving pins from tests.
caveats: ESP32 and ESP32-C3 only.
GUI-centric.
Serial needs com0com on Windows.
DIO/DOUT flash only.

candidates.name: Velxio (browser/Docker simulator whose ESP32 boards run on its own lcgamboa-derived QEMU tree, with an 'esp32s3-picsimlab' machine)
candidates.license: AGPL-3.0 with a paid commercial licence also offered. The QEMU engine (GPL-2.0) source is published as a tarball that needs a (free) velxio.dev licence key; it is not a public git repo. The native desktop app is a paid Pro feature (30-day trial).
candidates.latest_version: v3.0.5 (2026-09-02); prebuilt 'QEMU ESP32 Libraries (auto-built)' updated 2026-08-24. Espressif developer-blog article dated 2026-07-31.
candidates.summary: A web IDE plus circuit simulator. ESP32, ESP32-S3 and ESP32-C3 boards boot on libqemu-xtensa/riscv32 built from its own fork of lcgamboa/qemu, with callbacks for GPIO, UART, ADC, I2C, SPI, RMT and LEDC. Its docs say plain lcgamboa lacks the esp32s3-picsimlab machine and the S3 GPSPI model. Sketches are compiled internally with a pinned arduino-esp32 3.3.10 (IDF 5.5.4).

capabilities.detail: The app is AGPLv3 on GitHub. The QEMU engine is GPL-2.0, but its full source is available only as a download needing a velxio.dev licence key; the Docker image ships prebuilt .so files.

Supported boards include ESP32-S3 DevKit, XIAO ESP32-S3 and Arduino Nano ESP32, mapped to the 'esp32s3-picsimlab' machine. The worker code says the S3 machine 'models no radio', which contradicts the blog's Wi-Fi claim.
It compiles with a pinned arduino-esp32 3.3.10 / IDF 5.5.4; sketches that use APIs removed in 3.0 (e.g. ledcSetup/ledcAttachPin) are not supported. ESP-IDF projects go through its own wrapper.
No documented way to load an externally built firmware.bin or merged image; the backend compiles the sketch itself.

Serial is streamed over Velxio's WebSocket (/ws/sim/{board_id}, 'serial_output' and 'esp32_serial_input' messages) to the web Serial Monitor. No pyserial or TCP port is documented for the library mode; the UART-only fallback (EspQemuManager) runs QEMU as a subprocess with serial over TCP.

A source comment says 'the engine models the Serial-JTAG console', and the build forces ARDUINO_USB_CDC_ON_BOOT=1 / ARDUINO_USB_MODE=1 (HWCDC) for boards whose default is CDC on boot. USB-OTG/TinyUSB is not modelled. Not verified (CHƯA THỬ).
Per-channel LEDC duty is read about every 50 ms (duty_pct events), with LEDC→GPIO routing and a GPIO oscilloscope. There is no documented API giving pulse widths in µs.
The WebSocket message 'esp32_gpio_in' {pin, state}, or bridge.set_pin() in Python, drives GPIO inputs; UI buttons do the same.
The I2C bus is synchronous with virtual device responses (set_i2c_response), built-in slave models and WASM custom chips. AS5600, BNO085 and VL53L1X are not listed.
Not documented. The worker notes '-icount is off for Xtensa'.
Docker image with a FastAPI backend, WebSocket API, and an MCP server (compile_project, run_project, circuit tools). There is no documented headless test runner; it is UI-first.
Self-hosting runs in Docker (a Linux container). The native Windows desktop app is Pro (paid, 30-day trial). A Windows developer setup with an MSYS2-built libqemu-xtensa.dll is documented.
Simulator only.

candidates.fit: It is the only QEMU-based tool found that claims ESP32-S3 GPIO, LEDC and I2C models plus a USB-Serial-JTAG (HWCDC) console, so it may be interesting for manual exploration. However, it is an IDE that compiles its own pinned sketches, not PlatformIO builds. There is no pyserial port, the engine source is behind a licence key, and there is no CI test runner. Low fit for automated testing of this project.
caveats: Claims (S3 USJ console, LEDC, I2C) are taken from docs and code comments and are not verified.
AGPL plus commercial licensing; the desktop app is paid.
The multi-file PlatformIO project would need restructuring to build inside Velxio.
candidates.cost_notes: Self-host (Docker) and velxio.dev are free. Desktop/Pro is paid after a 30-day trial. A commercial licence is needed for closed-source use.

candidates.name: a159x36/qemu (community fork of espressif/qemu for LilyGO T-Display boards)
candidates.license: GPL-2.0 / LGPL-2.1 (QEMU)
candidates.latest_version: Default branch esp-develop-9.2; last commit 2026-07-07 ('Use 24 bits instead of 16 for st7789v display'). Release tags (e.g. v5.4.2, 2026-07-07) have no notes, and no binary assets were found.
candidates.summary: The fork's description is 'Qemu Emulator for TTGO TDisplay esp32 board'. Its esp32s3 machine is extended beyond Espressif's: GPIO model, LEDC (C3-style model), 2× MCPWM, SENS/touch, RMT, ULP, 2 I2C controllers with a TMP105 hard-wired at 0x48 and an MPU6050 at 0x68, a Wi-Fi MAC, and an ST7789 display skin with buttons on GPIO0 and GPIO14. It is not documented beyond the code.

capabilities.detail: Public GPL fork on GitHub.
The extended esp32s3 machine is board-specific (T-Display-S3 'skin') and undocumented.
No documentation.
Inferred: as a fork of espressif/qemu esp-develop-9.2 it boots a merged image through -drive if=mtd (CHƯA THỬ).
Uses inherited QEMU UART chardevs (e.g. -serial tcp::…); not tested.
Uses the same esp32c3_jtag stub type (TYPE_ESP32C3_JTAG).
The LEDC model computes on/off times and drives LED intensity and GPIO function signals. There is no documented host interface for measuring pulses.
A full GPIO model exists (gpio_in, 49 named input lines), but on S3 the inputs are wired only to the emulated display's buttons (GPIO0/GPIO14) and touch pads. There is no scripted API.
I2C0/I2C1 exist, but the only devices are hard-wired (tmp105@0x48, mpu6050@0x68); other sensors need C code.
esp_timg.c has the same CONF_UPDATE_EN latch, so S3 watchdogs are expected to behave as in Espressif QEMU (inferred from identical code).
Plain QEMU CLI and QMP, but you must build from source; no published binaries were found.
No Windows binaries or instructions.
Emulator only.

candidates.fit: Low fit. It shows that S3 GPIO, LEDC and I2C models exist in the community, but it is undocumented, board-specific (display and buttons) and not scriptable for pin injection. It has the same USB-JTAG and WDT limits as Espressif QEMU and no Windows binaries.
caveats: Undocumented and single-maintainer.
Hard-wired I2C devices.

candidates.name: Espressif esp-emulator ('esp-emu', Beta). Adjacent, NOT QEMU-based (Rust), listed because it is Espressif's newer emulator with ESP32-S3 support
candidates.license: The GitHub repo (installer, docs, helper tools) is Apache-2.0. The emulator ships as prebuilt binaries, and its Rust source is not in the repo.
candidates.summary: A Rust emulator for ESP32-C3/C5/C6/H2/P4/S31 and ESP32-S3; on S3 it runs the real ROM and bootloader up to a dual-core app_main. It lists models for UART, USB Serial JTAG, GPIO, systimer, timer groups, LEDC, PCNT, MCPWM, RMT, GP-SPI, I2C (with an EEPROM slave), eFuse, flash, PSRAM, and the TIMG and RTC watchdogs, plus Wi-Fi and BLE. CLI features include --uart-tcp, --control-tcp (reset, erase), --gdb, --timeout, --exit-on and --trace.

capabilities.detail: The repo 'distributes the installer, prebuilt release binaries, user-facing docs, and helper tools' (Apache-2.0). No public emulator source was found, even though install.sh mentions building from source.
Since 0.43.0: stock ESP-IDF images boot through ROM and bootloader to a dual-core app_main, with quad and octal PSRAM. 0.44.0 fixed QIO/QOUT boot asserts.
Only ESP-IDF-built merged images are documented; Arduino builds are CHƯA THỬ.
Takes any merged flash binary (--firmware) and reads the flash size from the image header. There is no PlatformIO integration (CHƯA THỬ with .pio outputs).

--uart-tcp HOST:PORT bridges UART0 to a TCP server (pyserial socket://); --uart1-tcp does the same for UART1. Also stdin/stdout and --inject/--inject-on. --control-tcp accepts reset, reset --soft, erase and write-region.

USB Serial JTAG is listed as modelled, and esptool/espefuse work over socket:// in USB-Serial-JTAG download mode (0.43.0). Whether an app's HWCDC console reaches the host at runtime is not documented (CHƯA THỬ). USB-OTG is not modelled.
LEDC, MCPWM and PCNT are listed as modelled, but there is no documented host way to observe pin waveforms or pulse widths.
GPIO is modelled, but no host command to drive a pin is documented; the control channel supports only reset, erase, write-region, efuse-load and ping.
HP I2C master with a built-in 24Cxx EEPROM slave at 0x50 (0.42.0); it can be swapped only through the internal Rust API. No sensor models.

TIMG and RTC watchdogs are modelled. 0.44.0 fixed the task WDT firing late or never ('[task_wdt] group passes on C3, C5 and P4'; S3 not listed) and fixed timekeeping across reboots. S3 panic/abort output includes backtraces. Reset and soft reset go through --control-tcp.
Headless CLI with --timeout, --exit-on and --inject, and --control-tcp built for pytest-embedded's hard_reset/erase; also --gdb and --trace. No account needed.
Binaries exist only for Linux x86_64/arm64, macOS arm64 and WASM. install.sh refuses Windows ('Build from source under WSL or native Windows'). WSL2 is the likely route (CHƯA THỬ).
Emulator only; it pairs with pytest-embedded as QEMU does.

candidates.fit: This is outside the strict QEMU area, but it is the most promising Espressif path for exactly what QEMU lacks on S3: a USB-Serial-JTAG model, GPIO, LEDC, I2C and working watchdogs. However, S3 support is only 11 days old (Beta), there is no native Windows build, and no host API to drive the E-stop GPIO or measure PWM is documented. It is worth one hands-on trial under WSL2, focused on the HWCDC transport and the TWDT.
caveats: Beta, releasing weekly.
The emulator source is not published.
S3 is the newest target.

report.notes:
Scope: Espressif QEMU and QEMU-based front-ends, checked 2026-09-29 against primary sources (GitHub releases, source at the release tags, official docs). The QEMU sources were read at tag esp-develop-9.2.2-20260417, and esp-develop head 2026-04-29 was diffed against it: the USB-JTAG stub and esp32s3.c are unchanged. Hands-on claims come from the orchestrator-provided run on this machine (29/09/2026). Items marked CHƯA THỬ have not been run.

Key findings:
1. Espressif QEMU is the only mature, free, native-Windows way to run this firmware without a board. On ESP32-S3 it covers the CPU, flash, UART0/1, SysTimer, timer groups, panic/restart and reset reasons. It does NOT cover USB-Serial-JTAG (a stub; HWCDC is unreachable, so a UART0 build env is needed), LEDC (not modelled on S3), GPIO input (only the strap register; the E-stop reads 'not pressed' forever), I2C/SPI/ADC/PCNT, or the RTC WDT.
2. A likely upstream bug: the S3 timer-group WDT never fires. QEMU's shared esp_timg.c latches the stage config only on CONF_UPDATE_EN (bit 22). ESP32-S3 WDTCONFIG0 bits 21-22 are reserved (ESP-IDF v5.5 soc header), and the S3 HAL never sets the bit in v4.4, v5.5 or master, while the C3 HAL does. This is worth an issue at espressif/qemu.
3. Documentation drift: the esp-toolchain-docs S3 README (last changed 2025-08-29) still says to use 'timer.esp32c3.timg', but the release uses 'timer.esp32s3.timg'; idf.py qemu passes timer.<target>.timg,wdt_disable=true by default. The feature table still shows SD/MMC ❌ for S3, although 20260417 added it.
4. Harness pattern: Espressif (ESP-IDF pytest 'qemu' marker) and arduino-esp32 use pytest-embedded with a merged image in QEMU and the same tests on hardware. arduino-esp32 has disabled its QEMU stage and lists only esp32/esp32c3 there; it prefers Wokwi. For this project: keep SerialVehicleIO as the client. Choose the transport per target: socket:// needs a draining adapter because in_waiting returns 0/1. -serial COMn with a com0com pair should give real COM semantics (Windows-only QEMU option, CHƯA THỬ). On a real board, use COMx.
5. QEMU-based front-ends: PICSimLab 0.9.3 (GPL-2.0) supports only ESP32 and ESP32-C3. Velxio v3.0.5 (AGPL plus commercial) has an 'esp32s3-picsimlab' machine claiming GPIO, LEDC, I2C and a Serial-JTAG console, but it is UI-first, compiles its own sketches, and its engine source needs a licence key. The a159x36 fork extends the S3 machine for T-Display boards and is undocumented. The ESP-IDF VS Code extension and Espressif-IDE have QEMU commands for ESP-IDF projects only. mluis/qemu-esp32 is an ESP32-only Docker wrapper. SimulIDE 2.0 tester builds have an ESP32 proof of concept that the maintainer calls 'not really usable' (forum, 2025-09-20).
6. Adjacent non-QEMU emulators with ESP32-S3 support, outside this area; please make sure another area covers them:
   - Espressif esp-emulator (esp-emu 0.44.0, 2026-09-25; S3 since 0.43.0): models USB Serial JTAG, GPIO, LEDC, I2C and WDTs. Linux/macOS/WASM only; emulator source not published.
   - joakimeriksson/esp32sim: MIT, Rust; claims S3 with USB-CDC, GPIO, I2C, timer groups and the RTC WDT.
   - danish9661/esp32s3-emulator: Rust/WASM, early stage.
   Wokwi's own docs do not describe it as QEMU-based.
7. Recommendation for this project, within this area:
   - Add a QEMU-only PlatformIO env with ARDUINO_USB_CDC_ON_BOOT=0 and either a DIO flash mode or a 16 MB merged image.
   - Script: merge the bins, start qemu-system-xtensa -nographic -machine esp32s3 -serial tcp::5555,server,nowait, then run the existing Python protocol tests. Optionally use pytest-embedded-qemu for lifecycle and QMP reset.
   - Keep PWM, E-stop, sensor and watchdog-timeout checks on host-side fakes and real hardware.
   - Label QEMU results as 'đã chạy trên giả lập' (ran in emulation), not hardware-verified.

verification.topic: Adversarial fact-check of the report 'Espressif QEMU and QEMU-based front-ends' for running the autopark ESP32-S3 Arduino firmware without hardware. Checked 2026-09-29 against GitHub source at tag esp-develop-9.2.2-20260417, release notes and the API, ESP-IDF source and docs, PyPI, and project docs. Two local read-only checks were run on the QEMU binary already downloaded at D:\xetulai\_platformio\qemu.

checks.claim: Latest release is esp-develop-9.2.2-20260417 (QEMU 9.2.2). It was tagged 2026-04-17 and published 2026-04-19, and it is still the latest on 2026-09-29.
The esp-develop head (2026-04-29) has no USB-JTAG, LEDC, I2C or WDT changes for S3.
checks.source: https://api.github.com/repos/espressif/qemu/compare/esp-develop-9.2.2-20260417...esp-develop (5 commits ahead: ESP32-C6 machine, a systimer debug trace and RISC-V fixes; esp32s3.c, esp32c3_jtag.c and esp_timg.c are untouched)

checks.claim: ESP-IDF tools.json recommends esp_develop_9.2.2_20260417 for esp32 and esp32s3, with a win64 entry.
checks.source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/espressif/esp-idf/master/tools/tools.json (the same entry is in release/v6.1 and release/v5.5)

checks.claim: The whole emulator is GPL-2.0, the ROMs such as pc-bios/esp32s3_rev0_rom.bin ship as blobs, and Espressif says it 'does not provide support for QEMU'.
S3 history: initial support in 9.0.0-20240606; quad/octal PSRAM, virtual RGB LCD and SHA-384/512 in 9.2.2-20250228; SDMMC, TIE fixes and the libiconv-2.dll fix in 9.2.2-20260417.

The machine is 'esp32s3' ('Espressif ESP32S3 machine', 2 CPUs by default). UART0 and UART1 are bound to serial_hd(0) and serial_hd(1); UART2 exists but has no chardev. It also has SDMMC, TWAI, OpenCores Ethernet and an RGB framebuffer.
Only 2, 4, 8 and 16 MB images are accepted. An 8 MB image gets the gd25q64 model, which lacks quad-enable, so a QIO build boot-loops; a 16 MB image gets is25lp128, which works.
checks.source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/espressif/qemu/esp-develop-9.2.2-20260417/hw/xtensa/esp32s3.c (the flash model is chosen by size: w25x16, gd25q32, gd25q64, is25lp128) ; https://raw.githubusercontent.com/espressif/qemu/esp-develop-9.2.2-20260417/hw/block/m25p80.c (quad-enable is handled only for Spansion, ISSI, Macronix and Winbond; GigaDevice has no handling)
checks.correction: This also applies to 4 MB images, which use the GigaDevice gd25q32 model. Espressif's own docs example uses --fill-flash-size 4MB. Only 2 MB (Winbond) and 16 MB (ISSI) images implement quad-enable.

checks.claim: pyserial's socket:// in_waiting returns only 0 or 1 because it is select-based.
checks.source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/pyserial/pyserial/master/serial/urlhandler/protocol_socket.py (returns len(lr) from select; pyserial 3.5 is still the latest on PyPI)

checks.claim: QEMU offers the Windows-only -serial COMn (host COM port).
checks.source: https://www.qemu.org/docs/master/system/invocation.html ; local check: qemu-system-xtensa.exe -chardev help (20260417 win64) lists serial, stdio, pipe, socket, file, udp and others

checks.claim: USB-Serial-JTAG is only a register stub, 'misc.esp32c3.usb_serial_jtag', at 0x60038000: reads return 0, writes are dropped, and it has no chardev. The docs mark USB ❌ on all targets.
LEDC is ❌ for S3. Its registers fall in the generic esp32s3.iomem region, where reads return 0 and writes are ignored silently.
Only the classic ESP32 machine has an LEDC model, added in 7.2.0-20230223. It only passes an integer duty % to LED devices.
checks.source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/espressif/qemu/esp-develop-9.2.2-20260417/hw/misc/esp32_ledc.c (led_set_intensity with a percentage; the tree has no esp32c3_ledc.c) ; 7.2.0-20230223 release notes

checks.claim: The GPIO model implements only GPIO_STRAP, and every other register reads 0. So an INPUT_PULLUP E-stop always reads LOW ('not pressed'), and there is no host API to drive a pin.
checks.source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/espressif/qemu/esp-develop-9.2.2-20260417/hw/gpio/esp32_gpio.c ; https://raw.githubusercontent.com/espressif/qemu/esp-develop-9.2.2-20260417/hw/gpio/esp32s3_gpio.c (an empty subclass that only sets strap_mode)

checks.claim: The esp32s3 machine creates no I2C or GP-SPI controller; there is only SPI1 for flash. The docs mark I2C, GP-SPI, I2S and RMT ❌, and ADC, PCNT and MCPWM are not listed.
The classic ESP32 machine has an 'undocumented' I2C controller with a TMP105 hard-wired at 0x48.
checks.correction: The TMP105 at 0x48 (25 °C) is correct. The controller is not undocumented, though: the esp-develop-20210220 release notes say 'Added I2C peripheral', and 8.0.0 fixed multi-byte I2C reads. Only the feature table marks I2C ❌ for ESP32.

checks.claim: esp_timg.c latches WDT stage config, stage values and prescaler only when a WDTCONFIG0 write has CONF_UPDATE_EN (bit 22) set.
On S3 silicon, WDTCONFIG0 bits 21-22 are reserved, the S3 HAL never sets conf_update_en (v4.4, v5.5 and master), and the C3 HAL does.
checks.correction: On master the S3 HAL has moved to components/esp_hal_wdt/esp32s3/include/hal/mwdt_ll.h, and it still has no conf_update_en. GitHub search found no existing espressif/qemu issue about it.

checks.claim: The docs name 'timer.esp32c3.timg', but the release's S3 timer groups are 'timer.esp32s3.timg'. idf.py qemu passes timer.<target>.timg,wdt_disable=true by default. The RTC WDT is not emulated.
Timers run on QEMU_CLOCK_VIRTUAL, with no -icount by default. -icount is deterministic but not cycle-accurate. Peripheral state survives a CPU-only reset.
checks.source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/espressif/qemu/esp-develop-9.2.2-20260417/hw/timer/esp_timg.c ; https://raw.githubusercontent.com/espressif/qemu/esp-develop-9.2.2-20260417/hw/timer/esp_systimer.c ; https://www.qemu.org/docs/master/system/invocation.html ; esp32s3.c esp32s3_soc_reset (only the interrupt matrix and UARTs are reset, and only on a PERIPH reset)

checks.claim: esptool cannot reset over TCP because RTS is not transmitted; use system_reset. The ESP-IDF Docker image installs qemu* via idf_tools. ESP-IDF's pytest.ini has a 'qemu' marker.
Every release ships an official x86_64-w64-mingw32 tarball.
checks.correction: Windows (and macOS or arm64) binaries first appear in esp-develop-8.1.3-20231206 ('Added binary releases for Windows...'). Releases 20200528 to 8.1.2-20231017 had only Linux or source tarballs. Every S3-capable release (9.0.0-20240606 and later) does include win64.

checks.claim: The 20260417 Windows build no longer needs libiconv-2.dll and runs as a static binary.
checks.source: 20260417 release notes ; local check: objdump -p D:\xetulai\_platformio\qemu\qemu\bin\qemu-system-xtensa.exe imports only Windows system DLLs (KERNEL32, WS2_32, msvcrt, ...). -accel help lists tcg only.

checks.claim: About 174 MB unpacked.
checks.correction: The unpacked folder is about 139 MiB: qemu-system-xtensa.exe and qemu-system-xtensaw.exe are 71.7 MB each, plus share/. 174 MiB is that folder plus the 36 MB .tar.xz archive.

checks.claim: Neither platformio/platform-espressif32 7.1.3 nor pioarduino 55.03.312 mentions QEMU.
checks.source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/pioarduino/platform-espressif32/main/platform.json (version 55.03.312, Arduino 3.3.12, IDF v5.5.5) ; https://raw.githubusercontent.com/platformio/platform-espressif32/develop/platform.json (7.1.3) ; builder/main.py, builder/frameworks/espidf.py, platform.py and README.md in both have 0 'qemu' hits (no full code search)

checks.claim: Merge the bins with esptool: merge_bin --fill-flash-size on v4, merge-bin --pad-to-size on v5. PlatformIO documents test_testing_command with qemu-riscv/HiFive1.
idf.py qemu is in code since ESP-IDF v5.3, S3 is documented since v5.4, and the stable docs are v6.1.
checks.source: https://api.github.com/repos/espressif/esp-idf/commits?path=tools/idf_py_actions/qemu_ext.py (added 2023-12-03; release/v5.2 has no qemu_ext.py) ; https://raw.githubusercontent.com/espressif/esp-idf/release/v5.4/docs/conf_common.py (v5.3 adds QEMU_DOCS only to ESP32 and C3) ; https://docs.espressif.com/projects/esp-idf/en/stable/esp32s3/api-guides/tools/qemu.html (RELEASE='v6.1'; v6.1 released 2026-08-27)

checks.claim: esp-toolchain-docs last changed 2025-09-11 (README) and 2025-08-29 (S3 README); the S3 SD/MMC row is stale.
arduino-esp32 docs say 'QEMU is only supported for ESP32 and ESP32-C3 targets'.
Hands-on: 'Incorrect size of core dump image: -65536' on a blank core-dump partition is harmless log noise.
checks.source: https://github.com/espressif/qemu/issues/169 ; https://raw.githubusercontent.com/espressif/qemu/esp-develop-9.2.2-20260417/hw/ssi/esp32s3_spi.c (esp32s3_spi_get_dummy: len = (cycles+7)/8, ignoring the number of data lines)
checks.correction: Open issue #169 (2026-09-02, tag 20260417) lists this exact symptom: 'the core-dump check reads a size of -65536 from erased flash'. The cause is an SPI1 dummy-cycle bug: runtime dual/quad-I/O reads (0xBB/0xEB) come back shifted by 2 bytes. Boot is unaffected.

checks.claim: Recommendation: a QEMU env with a DIO flash mode or a 16 MB merged image is enough.
checks.correction: Both options fix boot only. In DIO and QIO builds every runtime esp_flash_read (NVS/Preferences, LittleFS, OTA or core-dump reads) is corrupted: 'NVS re-initialises on every boot'. The fix is in open PR #177 (unmerged). DOUT/QOUT reads use single-line dummy cycles and may avoid the bug (inference, CHƯA THỬ). The current firmware src/ uses no NVS or filesystem; only the Arduino core's nvs_flash_init and the core-dump check touch it.

checks.claim: 2.9.3 (2026-08-31), Python ≥3.10, MIT, pytest-embedded-qemu depends on qemu.qmp==0.0.3.
QEMU_TARGETS includes esp32s3 (strap 0x07). The default args are '-nographic -machine {target}'. The DUT writes to QEMU stdin and reads stdout, and hard_reset sends QMP system_reset.
The eFuse helper uses pexpect.spawn, which is unavailable on Windows.
arduino-esp32 runs '--embedded-services esp,arduino,wokwi,qemu' and pins 2.8.1 (and esptool 5.3.1).

QEMU_TEST_TARGETS is esp32 and esp32c3 only. The QEMU stage is disabled (qemu_enabled=false; 'redundant with most of the Wokwi tests'). It runs on ubuntu-latest with Linux tarballs, uses '-machine $target -m 4M -nographic' for Xtensa, and adds '-icount 3' for RISC-V.
Only the timer, ticker, hash, fs, unity, multitasking and hello_world tests are eligible for QEMU.
checks.source: https://api.github.com/repos/espressif/arduino-esp32/contents/tests/validation?ref=master ; https://raw.githubusercontent.com/espressif/arduino-esp32/master/.github/scripts/tests_run.sh (a test is skipped only if its ci.yml sets false)
checks.correction: eeprom and network_client also have no ci.yml, so they are eligible too. The gpio, i2c_master, adc_pwm, uart and other tests set qemu: false.

checks.claim: The arduino-esp32 repository is LGPL-2.1.
0.9.3 was released 2026-09-20 with win64 setup/zip builds and a PICSimLab_NOGUI AppImage. PICSimLab-rcontrol is 0.9.2 (2026-06-20).
The only ESP boards are ESP32_DevKitC and ESP32_C3_DevKitC_02, there is no S3 picsimlab machine, and only DIO/DOUT flash is supported.
Backend lcgamboa/qemu picsimlab-esp32: last commit 2026-09-19, 'Updated to use qemu-esp32 0.9.2'.
checks.correction: The date is right, but the head commit on 2026-09-19 is 'Merge pull request #6 from fariouche/picsimlab-esp32' (Wi-Fi descriptor support). The branch was rebased onto esp-develop-9.2 on 2026-07-30.

checks.claim: v3.0.5 (2026-09-02); QEMU libraries rebuilt 2026-08-24. License is AGPLv3 plus a paid commercial licence. The QEMU engine source (GPL-2.0) is a tarball that needs a velxio.dev licence key. The desktop app is Pro with a 30-day trial.

The compiler forces ARDUINO_USB_CDC_ON_BOOT=1 and ARDUINO_USB_MODE=1 because 'the engine models the Serial-JTAG console'. It pins arduino-esp32 3.3.10 on IDF 5.5.4, and plain lcgamboa lacks the esp32s3-picsimlab machine.
The worker says the S3 machine 'models no radio', which contradicts the blog's Wi-Fi claim.
checks.correction: The blog's Wi-Fi section and its 'Wi-Fi + full GPIO' row refer to the ESP32 (LX6) DevKit. The S3 boards are listed only with 'Hardware SPI (GPSPI2) peripherals', so there is no contradiction.

checks.claim: The extended S3 machine has a TMP105 at 0x48, an MPU6050 at 0x68, a C3-style LEDC, 2×MCPWM, RMT, ULP and a Wi-Fi MAC. It keeps the esp32c3_jtag stub and the same CONF_UPDATE_EN latch in esp_timg.c.
No binary assets were found; there are no Windows binaries, so you must build from source.
checks.correction: Releases v5.4.1 (2026-06-29), v5.3.1 (2026-02-10) and v5.1.11 include qemu-xtensa-softmmu tarballs for x86_64-w64-mingw32, x86_64-linux-gnu and macOS arm64/x86_64. v5.3.1 also ships ttgo-tdisplay-emulator packages, including windows_amd64. Only the newest tag, v5.4.2 (2026-07-07), has no assets. A 2026-06-17 commit fixed the Windows build.

checks.claim: Last commit 2026-07-07: 'Use 24 bits instead of 16 for st7789v display'.
checks.correction: The head commit on 2026-07-07 is 'Fix LCD display on s3 when using old IDF'.

checks.claim: 0.44.0 is dated 2026-09-25, and ESP32-S3 was added in 0.43.0 (2026-09-18). 0.44.0 fixed QIO/QOUT boot asserts, and its [task_wdt] fix lists C3, C5 and P4, not S3.
Binaries exist only for Linux x86_64/arm64, macOS arm64 and WASM; install.sh refuses Windows. The repo is Apache-2.0 and contains no emulator source.
LEDC, USB Serial JTAG and the RTC WDT are modelled (applied to S3).
checks.correction: The README's peripheral list does not say which chip has which peripheral. The 0.43.0 S3 notes name only timers, interrupts, GPIO, PCNT, MCPWM, GDMA, eFuse and flash encryption, plus Wi-Fi, BLE and PSRAM, and USB-Serial-JTAG only for download mode. S3 LEDC, the runtime USJ console and the S3 RTC WDT are unconfirmed.

missed_facts.fact: Open issue #169 (2026-09-02, tested on tag esp-develop-9.2.2-20260417) and open fix PR #177 (2026-09-08): the S3 SPI1 model counts dummy cycles as if on one line, so runtime quad/dual-I/O flash reads (0xEB/0xBB) return data shifted by 2 bytes. Reported effects: 'NVS re-initialises on every boot', LittleFS 'Corrupted dir pair', and core-dump size -65536. Boot is unaffected. The source line is `*len = (dummy_count + 7) / 8;` in esp32s3_spi_get_dummy. Neither the issue nor the PR has any maintainer reply. Any future Preferences, NVS or filesystem feature cannot be trusted in QEMU with DIO or QIO builds.

Open issue #175 (2026-09-08, tag 20260417): -machine esp32s3 dies with SIGSEGV in generated code under the default multi-threaded TCG (default when -icount is off) when the host is busy. The reporter saw about 1 in 15 runs with 14 parallel boots; it is 'not happening at all' with -accel tcg,thread=single. Their setup had out-of-tree devices. This matters for parallel CI; consider thread=single (CHƯA THỬ for timing impact).

Open issue #99 (2024-07-11, 'ESP32-S3 Blink not working', no maintainer reply): an Arduino sketch built with IDF 4.4.8 boot-loops on the S3 machine with an assert. This is an independent public report consistent with the hands-on QIO/GigaDevice quad-enable failure; it is unresolved after two years.

Open, unmerged community PR #173 (2026-09-05; the author calls it 'vibey') adds an S3 USB-OTG (DWC2) CDC-ACM model on serial_hd(2). That path is TinyUSB CDC (ARDUINO_USB_MODE=0), not USB-Serial-JTAG/HWCDC (USB_MODE=1), so even if merged it would not reach the production build's Serial.

The unreleased ESP32-C6 machine on esp-develop (2026-04-29) contains a TX-only USB-Serial-JTAG model with a chardev (EP1 writes go to qemu_chr_fe_write; there is no RX). It is not in any release and not on S3, but it is a small template for a local S3 patch.

The S3 machine writes the signature 0x51454d55 ('QEMU') at APB_CTRL base + 0x3F8 (0x600263F8), which lets firmware detect QEMU at runtime. A single build could then send the protocol to UART0 (Serial0) only under QEMU and keep HWCDC on hardware. Check what that address reads on real silicon first (CHƯA THỬ).

Inference from source (CHƯA THỬ): QEMU latches the WDT config only when a WDTCONFIG0 write sets bit 22. A QEMU-only test build that, after esp_task_wdt_init, unlocks WKEY (0x50D83AA1) and rewrites TIMG0/TIMG1 WDTCONFIG0 with bit 22 set should make the TWDT and IWDT fire in emulation. Never ship this, because bit 22 is reserved on S3 silicon.
QEMU's -snapshot, or snapshot=on on the -drive, stops writes from going back to the flash image, so you do not need a fresh copy per run (CHƯA THỬ with if=mtd).

On S3, IO_MUX (0x60009000) and RMT are registered as QEMU 'unimplemented devices', so -d unimp logs their accesses. GPIO-matrix and LEDC writes stay silent. Pin reconfiguration by the panic hook is therefore partly traceable (IO_MUX only; CHƯA THỬ).

The silent read-as-zero region 0x60000000-0x600D0FFF also covers I2C0 (0x60013000), PCNT (0x60017000) and APB_SARADC (0x60040000). Future drivers that poll done or status bits there will see 0 forever, so they may time out or spin instead of failing cleanly (inference). Sensor and ADC code paths need host fakes.

The PlatformIO registry has no package for Espressif's xtensa QEMU; tool-qemu-xtensa returns 404. Only platformio/tool-qemu-riscv exists, last updated 2020-07-05. The binary must come from the GitHub release or from idf_tools.py (install: on_request).
Open issue #166 (2026-08-02): ESP32-S3 PIE instructions EE.SLCXXP.2Q/EE.SRCXXP.2Q do not mask their argument and can terminate QEMU. This only matters if SIMD code such as esp-dsp is used later.

verification.overall:
The report holds up on the points that decide feasibility, checked against source at tag esp-develop-9.2.2-20260417, which is still the newest release and tag on 2026-09-29:
- USB-Serial-JTAG is a stub (reads 0, writes dropped, no chardev), so the production HWCDC build cannot be reached.
- LEDC, I2C, GP-SPI, PCNT and ADC fall in a silent read-as-zero region.
- GPIO is strap-only, so the E-stop always reads LOW ('not pressed').
- Only UART0 and UART1 reach the host.
- The S3 timer-group watchdogs never fire: esp_timg.c latches config only on CONF_UPDATE_EN (bit 22), which is reserved on S3 and never set by the S3 HAL in IDF v4.4, v5.5 or master.
- The flash-size and quad-enable explanation for the QIO boot-loop is also confirmed at source level.
Nearly all versions and dates are correct: QEMU release and tools.json, idf.py qemu history, pytest-embedded 2.9.3, arduino-esp32 3.3.12 and 4.0.0-RC1, PICSimLab 0.9.3, Velxio 3.0.5, esp-emu 0.43/0.44 and the docs dates.

The refutations are mostly minor:
- Windows binaries exist only since 8.1.3-20231206, not in every release.
- The unpacked size is about 139 MiB; 174 MiB includes the archive.
- The classic-ESP32 I2C controller does appear in release notes.
- Two quoted commit messages are wrong.
- The Velxio 'blog contradiction' does not exist.
- The list of QEMU-eligible arduino-esp32 tests misses eeprom and network_client.
- One refutation affects the comparison: a159x36/qemu does publish Linux, macOS and Windows binaries (v5.1.11 to v5.4.1). It is a native-Windows fork with S3 GPIO, LEDC and I2C models, though it is still undocumented, has no pin-injection API, and keeps the same USB-JTAG stub and watchdog latch.

The most important omission is open issue #169 / unmerged PR #177. On this release, every runtime dual- or quad-I/O flash read on S3 is shifted by 2 bytes: NVS re-initialises, LittleFS reports corruption, and the core-dump size reads -65536, which is the message the hands-on run called harmless. The report's advice to use a DIO build or a 16 MB QIO image therefore fixes boot only. The firmware's src/ uses no NVS or filesystem today, so the protocol results stand, but any stored configuration would be unreliable in emulation.

Other omissions:
- Open issue #175: esp32s3 SIGSEGV under the default multi-threaded TCG when the host is busy (-accel tcg,thread=single avoids it). This matters for parallel CI.
- Open issue #99: Arduino S3 boot-loop, reported in 2024 and unanswered.
- 4 MB images hit the same GigaDevice quad-enable gap.
- PR #173 adds USB-OTG CDC, not USB-JTAG, so it would not help HWCDC.
- A 'QEMU' signature register lets firmware detect emulation at runtime.
- -snapshot avoids writing back to the flash image.

Conclusion: Espressif QEMU remains a valid free, native-Windows way to run main.cpp and test the protocol in a UART0 build. It cannot cover USB-CDC, PWM, E-stop, sensors, watchdog timeouts or reliable runtime flash reads.

verified.title: Test harnesses that span simulation and real hardware

report.topic: Test harnesses that span simulation and real hardware (ESP32-S3, Arduino-ESP32 2.0.17 built with PlatformIO, HWCDC binary protocol). Researched and partly verified on this Windows 11 PC on 2026-09-29.

candidates.name: pytest-embedded (Espressif) + plugins: serial, serial-esp (esp), arduino, qemu, wokwi, jtag, idf, espemu, nuttx
candidates.license: MIT for all pytest-embedded packages. The backends it drives are licensed separately: Espressif QEMU is GPL-2.0 (open source); Wokwi simulates on closed-source cloud servers (only the wokwi-client library is open, MIT); esptool is GPL-2.0+.
candidates.latest_version: 2.9.3 (PyPI, 2026-08-31). main branch commit 2633b01 is dated 2026-09-29. Recent changes: 2.8.0 (2026-05-15) Wokwi custom chips; 2.8.1 (2026-06-16) Wokwi USB Serial JTAG and Arduino fast flashing; 2.9.0 (2026-08-25) new espemu service.
candidates.summary: A family of pytest plugins. Each test gets a `dut` object with pexpect-style expect()/write() and a Unity-output parser. The backend is chosen per run with --embedded-services, so the same test file can run on: a real chip (esp,arduino: auto-flash with esptool, then read the serial port), Espressif QEMU (qemu), Wokwi (arduino,wokwi), or any pyserial URL (serial). It supports several DUTs at once (--count) and writes JUnit reports.

capabilities.detail: The plugins are MIT (pyproject classifiers). Only the Wokwi backend is closed-source SaaS. The Python client it uses is open (MIT) and uploads the firmware to the Wokwi cloud.

Real hardware: esptool target esp32s3. QEMU: esp32s3 is in QEMU_TARGETS. Verified 2026-09-29 with Espressif QEMU 9.2.2 on Windows: the ESP32-S3 images booted, dut.hard_reset() worked through QMP, and a PlatformIO-built Unity image ran. Wokwi: esp32s3 maps to board-esp32-s3-devkitc-1 (not run here, no token). espemu cannot be used: it supports only RISC-V chips (c3/c5/c6/h2/p4/s31).

The arduino service reads an Arduino build directory: <sketch>.ino.bin or .ino.merged.bin, build.options.json (fqbn; the target is its 3rd field) and flash_args. It then flashes each part with esptool; fast --diff-with flashing arrived in 2.8.1. It does not depend on the core version. Verified: a 2.0.17 build, repackaged into that layout, is accepted (target esp32s3). The arduino-esp32 project's own CI uses this service for core 3.x/master.

There is no native PlatformIO support. Verified: a ~60-line shim is enough. It copies firmware.bin/.elf, bootloader.bin, partitions.bin and boot_app0.bin, writes build.options.json {fqbn: esp32:esp32:esp32s3} and flash_args (dio/80m/8MB, offsets 0x0/0x8000/0xe000/0x10000), and creates the merged image with esptool merge-bin. The qemu service also accepts any merged image through --qemu-image-path. Another route: flash with `pio run -t upload`, then run with --embedded-services esp or serial and --skip-autoflash.

The serial service opens --port with pyserial serial_for_url, so COMx, socket:// and rfc2217:// all work. dut.serial.proc is the pyserial object. Inside `with dut.serial.disable_redirect_thread():` the project's own client (e.g. SerialVehicleIO) has the port to itself. Verified on Windows against QEMU -serial tcp: the object is serial.urlhandler.protocol_socket.Serial. Gotcha (verified): pyserial's socket:// in_waiting only ever returns 0 or 1, and the background reader polls read_all() every 50 ms. The dut.expect path therefore runs at about 20 B/s over socket://. rfc2217:// keeps a real buffer and does not have this problem. The Wokwi backend has no pyserial object: bytes go out through dut.write() / wokwi.client.serial_write() and come back raw in the expect buffer.

Wokwi backend: `--wokwi-usb-serial-jtag true` (since 2.8.1) sets serialInterface=USB_SERIAL_JTAG on the board and removes the $serialMonitor wires. Wokwi's docs mark ESP32-S3 'USB Serial + JTAG: Serial supported, JTAG not', so the unmodified HWCDC firmware should be usable. This was not run here because it needs a token. QEMU backend: the console is UART0 on stdio only; the USB-CDC build showed only ROM and panic text. Real board: one USB-Serial-JTAG COM port carries both flashing (esptool) and the console.

The harness itself cannot measure PWM. Wokwi backend: wokwi.client.read_vcd()/save_vcd() return the logic-analyzer part's capture (8 channels, 1 GHz). read_pin() and listen_pin() give pin state and change events. QEMU backend: nothing. Real board: nothing built in; add sigrok-cli with an FX2 analyzer in a fixture.

Wokwi: wokwi.client.set_control('btn1','pressed',1/0), as used by arduino-esp32's GPIO test. QEMU: the plugin offers no GPIO stimulus, only QMP. Real board: needs an external relay or GPIO adapter, or a second board as a jig (multi-DUT).

Wokwi: built-in parts (e.g. the DS1307 used in arduino-esp32's i2c_master test) plus custom chips. Since 2.8.0 the plugin uploads chips/*.chip.json + .wasm, or [[chip]] entries from wokwi.toml. None of MT6701, AS5600, BNO085 or VL53L1X was checked as a built-in part. QEMU and real hardware: the harness provides nothing (--qemu-extra-args can pass extra QEMU arguments).

The harness only sees console text (asserts, backtraces, 'rst:0x.. (REASON)'). Reset methods: esptool hard_reset on real hardware; QMP system_reset on QEMU (verified, comes back as rst:0x1 POWERON); not implemented for Wokwi (use client.restart_simulation). The Wokwi client can pause, resume and wait_until_simulation_time() for deterministic timing. Panic decoding exists only in the idf plugin. How faithful esp_timer, TWDT and LEDC-after-CPU-reset are depends on the backend. Verified in QEMU: the project build's panic path prints assert + backtrace and reboots with rst:0xc (RTC_SW_CPU_RST).

Plain pytest CLI. expect_unity_test_output() writes one JUnit record per Unity case (verified: 3 cases recorded from a PlatformIO Unity image). Multi-DUT and sharding (--parallel-count) are supported. QEMU and real hardware need no account. Wokwi needs WOKWI_CLI_TOKEN and internet; CI minutes per month are Free 50, Hobby/Hobby+ 200, Pro 2000.

Verified 2026-09-29 on Windows 11 with Python 3.12.10: pip install of 2.9.3 (core, serial, serial-esp, arduino, qemu, wokwi) succeeded. The qemu and serial (socket://) services ran real tests. The arduino+wokwi services loaded and stopped with 'Set WOKWI_CLI_TOKEN'. Upstream CI runs only on Linux (self-hosted multiboard runners), so Windows is not officially tested. The Wokwi README does give PowerShell setup steps.

`--embedded-services esp,arduino --port COMx` auto-flashes with esptool, then runs the same test. Since 2.2.0 it reconnects if the serial port disappears, which helps with USB ports that re-enumerate on reset. arduino-esp32 runs the same test files on its GitLab hardware runners.

candidates.fit: This is the best fit and the only candidate that runs the same pytest file on a real ESP32-S3, on Wokwi and on QEMU; arduino-esp32's own CI already works this way. For this firmware, Wokwi (with --wokwi-usb-serial-jtag) is the only backend that can exercise the unmodified HWCDC protocol, the E-stop input and the PWM outputs (via VCD) today. QEMU is only useful for UART0 variant builds. The real board later only needs different services and port. Still needed: a small PlatformIO-to-Arduino-layout shim and a project fixture layer for transport, E-stop and PWM probing.
candidates.cost_notes: Free (MIT). Wokwi backend: a free account token. Free plan 50 CI minutes/month, Hobby/Hobby+ 200, Pro 2000; Pro costs €20/seat/month on annual billing (docs and pricing page read 2026-09-29). QEMU and real hardware: no cost.
caveats: The Wokwi backend was not run here (no token). The firmware is uploaded to the Wokwi cloud, and Espressif's own Wokwi page warns: 'Simulation results may differ from real hardware.' (https://docs.espressif.com/projects/esp-idf/en/stable/esp32s3/third-party-tools/wokwi.html).

QEMU on this PC: the unmodified project build (Arduino 2.0.17, default QIO) hits assert(flash_ret == ESP_OK) after esp_flash_init_default_chip (ESP-IDF v4.4 startup.c:328) and boot-loops. A DIO build with UART0 console works. In 5 of 24 boots of that same DIO build on this loaded host, it stalled right after the bootloader 'entry' line. Use timeouts plus a retry (arduino-esp32 retries each failed test once).
Throughput over socket://: when dut.expect() reads through the redirect thread, it gets about 20 B/s. For bulk or binary traffic, use disable_redirect_thread() or rfc2217://.

Tests that use the `wokwi` fixture (set_control, read_pin) cannot run on hardware as they are. arduino-esp32 marks such tests `platforms: hardware: false`, or guards them (the nvs test skips hard_reset when there is no serial port). A project-level abstraction is required.
espemu (esp-emu, added in 2.9.0) supports RISC-V chips only, not the ESP32-S3.
Panic and core-dump decoding lives in pytest-embedded-idf and applies to ESP-IDF apps only. For Arduino builds, decode backtraces yourself with addr2line.

candidates.name: arduino-esp32 runtime test pipeline (tests/validation + .github/scripts/tests_run.sh, socs_config.sh, workflows tests_hw_wokwi.yml / tests_qemu.yml)
candidates.license: Repository LGPL-2.1. It runs on pytest-embedded (MIT). The hardware lab is internal to Espressif (GitLab).
candidates.latest_version: master at commit 6cddb19 (2026-09-29). Core tags: 3.3.12 (stable), 4.0.0-RC1 and 4.0.0-alpha1 (pre-releases). tests/requirements.txt pins pytest-embedded-* 2.8.1 and esptool 5.3.1.
candidates.summary: Each test is a sketch plus test_<name>.py, with an optional ci.yml (per-platform/target flags, FQBN matrix) and diagram.<chip>.json. Sketches are built once with arduino-cli. tests_run.sh then runs the same pytest file on one of three platforms. Hardware (default): `--embedded-services esp,arduino`, jobs in the GitLab lab, gated by a hil_test label. -W: `--embedded-services arduino,wokwi --wokwi-diagram diagram.<chip>.json`, jobs on GitHub Actions with WOKWI_CLI_TOKEN. -Q: `--embedded-services qemu --qemu-image-path <sketch>.ino.merged.bin`, disabled by default. A failed test is retried once.

capabilities.detail: The scripts and workflows are public (LGPL-2.1). The Wokwi backend is closed, and the hardware lab is internal to Espressif.
esp32s3 is in HW_TEST_TARGETS and WOKWI_TEST_TARGETS. QEMU_TEST_TARGETS contains only esp32 and esp32c3.
It tests the core itself (current master, 3.x/4.x) built with arduino-cli, not 2.0.x.
The scripts expect arduino-cli build directories ($HOME/.arduino/tests/<target>/<sketch>/build.tmp with sdkconfig, merged.bin, flash_args).
Communication goes through pytest-embedded: dut.expect/write, plus wokwi.client.serial_write for synchronisation acknowledgements. No binary protocol tests at the pyserial level were seen.
Wokwi diagrams wire the UART to $serialMonitor. `--wokwi-usb-serial-jtag true` is added only for esp32p4, and only outside CI.

The adc_pwm test (LEDC) runs on hardware only: ci.yml sets `wokwi: false, qemu: false` because SigmaDelta is not simulated. It checks through the API (ledcReadFreq and similar), not by measuring the pin.
The gpio test presses a Wokwi pushbutton with set_control and reads an LED with read_pin. It runs on Wokwi only (ci.yml: hardware false, qemu false).
The i2c_master test uses the Wokwi DS1307 part and runs on Wokwi only (hardware false, qemu false).

The timer Unity test has no ci.yml, so it runs on every platform. power_management (reset reason, TWDT feed, deep sleep) is hardware-only: Wokwi RTC is only partial and QEMU is not supported. The nvs test calls dut.serial.hard_reset() only when a serial port exists, so that step is skipped on Wokwi.

Orchestrated by GitHub Actions, with GitLab for hardware. Secrets: WOKWI_CLI_TOKEN and GITLAB_ACCESS_TOKEN. QEMU binaries come from espressif/qemu releases. Results from all platforms are aggregated and missing tests are reported explicitly.
The scripts use bash, yq and arduino-cli and run on ubuntu-latest and GitLab Linux runners. No Windows procedure is documented.
The same test files run on physical boards: GitLab jobs are assigned to runners by chip tags.

candidates.fit: This is not a tool to install but a reference design to copy: one pytest file per test, platform flags per test, Unity on the device with pytest on the host, and a retry-once policy. It also proves that one test file can serve hardware, Wokwi and QEMU. Its scripts assume arduino-cli and Linux, so a PlatformIO + Windows project should reimplement the small runner in Python.
candidates.cost_notes: Free. Wokwi minutes follow the Wokwi plan. Espressif's hardware lab is not available to outside projects.
caveats: QEMU is disabled by default. CI_README says 'Wokwi simulator can cover most of what QEMU does'.
Tests that depend on stimulus are marked hardware:false, so on real boards those behaviours stay untested; equivalent hardware tests need separate means.

candidates.name: PlatformIO Unit Testing (pio test: Unity/GoogleTest/doctest, native env, test_testing_command for simulators, custom test runner, pio remote test)
candidates.license: PlatformIO Core is Apache-2.0. PIO Remote needs a PlatformIO Account (free registration, cloud service).
candidates.latest_version: PlatformIO Core 6.2.0 (2026-09-05). It fixed a Windows unit-testing failure around Serial.end() and a bug where the test-suite status was hard-coded as PASSED.
candidates.summary: PlatformIO builds a separate test firmware for each test/ folder. It then either uploads it and parses Unity/GoogleTest/doctest output from test_port, or runs a test_testing_command (documented examples: QEMU, Renode, simavr; use --without-uploading) and parses its stdout. Other options: a native env for host tests; test_framework=custom with test_custom_runner.py to take over the testing stage in Python; `pio remote test` to use a board attached to a remote agent.

capabilities.detail: Core is Apache-2.0. Remote testing uses PlatformIO's cloud and requires an account.

On a real board it is supported (espressif32 platform, embedded Unity). In simulation, verified 2026-09-29: Unity tests for esp32-s3-devkitc-1 ran in Espressif QEMU 9.2.2 through test_testing_command on Windows (3/3 PASS, 8.4 s, JUnit written, QEMU killed afterwards). This needed three changes: a post-build merge script, a UART0 console (ARDUINO_USB_CDC_ON_BOOT=0) and board_build.flash_mode=dio. With the default QIO mode the image asserted and `pio test` hung.
Verified with espressif32@7.1.3 (Arduino-ESP32 2.0.17). Arduino-ESP32 3.x through pioarduino was not tested here.
Built into PlatformIO.

The runner only parses test-framework text: either from test_port, which it opens with pyserial serial_for_url (so URL ports are accepted by the code, untested), or from the test program's stdout. To drive the binary protocol from Python you need test_custom_runner.py.
Real board: test_port can be the USB-Serial-JTAG COM port (not tested here). QEMU: UART0 only; the QEMU env needed ARDUINO_USB_CDC_ON_BOOT=0.
It cannot observe pins. A test can only check what the test firmware itself reads back.
There is no stimulus API. On real hardware, only external wiring or loopback can drive inputs.
It has no simulated sensors. Driver logic can be tested off-target in the native env with mocks: GoogleTest/gMock supports mocking, and the docs link an Arduino-Mock example.

On-target Unity can test esp_timer and the reset reason. Verified in QEMU: a 10 ms periodic esp_timer fired 20±3 times in 200 ms, and esp_reset_reason() was not UNKNOWN. A panic or WDT reset ends the Unity run, and PlatformIO has no multi-stage runner. There is also no test timeout option: a boot-looping image hung `pio test` until it was killed (observed after 100 s).
Headless CLI with --junit-output-path and --json-output-path (JUnit verified) and filters. No account needed, except for pio remote.
Verified: pio test with QEMU works on Windows 11 with PlatformIO 6.2.0. On Windows the runner uses the asyncio Proactor event loop.
`pio test -e <board env>` builds, uploads and reads test_port. `pio remote test` does the same on a remote agent.

candidates.fit: A useful complement, not the whole answer. The same Unity test sources can run in a QEMU env now (verified) and on the board later with `pio test -e esp32s3`, without extra Python. But it tests a special test firmware, not the production firmware end to end, and it cannot press the E-stop or measure PWM. Unity images built by PlatformIO can also be run by pytest-embedded's qemu service; this was verified, with per-case JUnit.
candidates.cost_notes: Free. PIO Remote requires a free PlatformIO Account.

candidates.license: LGPL-2.1

capabilities.detail: LGPL-2.1.

There is no ESP32 or esptool driver in labgrid/driver; flashing would need FlashScriptDriver or a custom driver. QEMUDriver builds generic command lines (flash as if=pflash, serial over a UNIX socket), so ESP32-S3 QEMU would need extra_args. Not tested.
It works with any firmware that talks over a console, but has no Arduino build or flash integration.
No integration. A custom driver would have to call pio or esptool.
SerialDriver works over RawSerialPort, USBSerialPort or NetworkSerialPort (RFC2217) and offers expect().
On real hardware the USB-Serial-JTAG port can be matched as a USB serial port (udev, Linux). Not available in simulation.
On real hardware, SigrokDriver.capture()/analyze() runs sigrok-cli protocol decoders (e.g. pwm). Not available in simulation.
On real hardware it can drive inputs with GpioDigitalOutputDriver (SysfsGPIO on a Linux exporter), HID relays or Modbus coils. Not available in simulation.
No sensor simulation.
Only generic tools: power cycling, console expect, and sigrok timing on real hardware. Nothing MCU-specific.
pytest plugin, labgrid-client CLI and coordinator. No account needed.
The maintainer (2023-03-01) said labgrid expects a POSIX system and recommended WSL instead of native Windows. The install docs cover Debian.
Real hardware is its main purpose (remote board farms).

candidates.cost_notes: Free. The hardware rig (Pi, relay, logic analyzer) is extra.
